title: ACC-71 Entitlement qualification → grant, deny or pending
summary: Establish whether a right actually exists, as a state distinct from being eligible for one or having paid toward one.

distinctFrom.because: Eligibility asks whether the rules would permit this. Entitlement asks whether it has been granted. ACQ-06's own guardrail names the difference; this journey is the state on the other side of it.

title: ACC-72 Entitlement grant → provision → verify availability
summary: Hold the distance between a right being granted and the thing behind it actually working.

title: ACC-73 Entitlement change → recalculate scope → expand, reduce or preserve
summary: Apply only the difference between the old and new rights, rather than re-applying a whole scope over a working one.

title: ACC-74 Entitlement loss → revoke future capability → reconcile existing obligations
summary: Stop future use of a right that has ended without cancelling what was validly created while it was held.

distinctFrom.because: Suspension restricts a right that still exists and is designed to come back. This is the right ending, which is why it reconciles obligations rather than holding them.

title: ACC-75 Access request → authorization check → allow, deny or step up
summary: Decide at the moment of the attempt whether this actor may take this action on this resource.

distinctFrom.because: Approval is a business decision taken in advance about a subject. Authorization is a runtime decision taken at the moment of the attempt, and being approved for something does not authorise every action within it.

title: ACC-76 Credential issued → activate → use, expire or revoke
summary: Run an access artifact through its own validity lifecycle, separately from the right it represents.

distinctFrom.because: The entitlement is the right. The credential is an artifact that presents it. Treating the artifact as the right means revoking a token looks like removing a benefit.

title: ACC-77 Credential compromise or revocation → disable → replace or re-authenticate
summary: Take a credential out of use immediately, and let any replacement come through its own authorised path.

title: ACC-78 Access suspension → restricted state → restore or terminate
summary: Restrict defined capabilities for a reason, in the smallest scope that addresses it, while keeping restoration genuinely possible.

distinctFrom.because: Grace continues a right whose validity has ended. Suspension restricts a right that is still valid. One is continuity after an ending; the other is a hold before one.

title: ACC-79 Capability restoration → revalidate → restore safely
summary: Rebuild access from what is currently valid, rather than replaying the capability set someone used to have.

distinctFrom.because: TIM-68 reverses a transition within a window and asks what side effects can be undone. This rebuilds a capability set from scratch against current conditions, with no assumption that the previous set is the target.

title: ACC-80 Deprovision request → dependency check → remove, retain or escalate
summary: Remove a capability that is no longer authorised, after establishing that nothing still depends on the thing being removed.

distinctFrom.because: ACC-74 ends a right and stops future use. This removes the technical resource behind it, which is a separate operation with its own failure modes and its own reasons to wait.

title: ACQ-01 Anonymous intent → known identity → qualified entry
summary: Carry a meaningful but anonymous intent signal through identity resolution without inventing an identity, and decide lifecycle entry as a question separate from having resolved one.

distinctFrom.because: ACQ-02 starts from something the person declared. Here nothing has been declared, so identity and permission both have to be established rather than read.

title: ACQ-02 Captured interest → qualification → appropriate destination
summary: Route first-party interest to the destination its own content justifies, instead of treating every capture as either a sales lead or a subscriber.

distinctFrom.because: This journey decides where interest goes. ACQ-09 is one of the places it can go, and owns the bounded window that follows - keeping both here would put the same window in two state machines.

title: ACQ-03 Intent escalation → higher-intent journey handoff
summary: Move ownership when someone in a low-intent lifecycle does something that no longer fits it, and make sure the journey being left behind actually goes quiet.

distinctFrom.because: ACQ-08 fires when a destination has been reached and acquisition is finished. This fires while everything is still in progress and only the ranking has changed.

title: ACQ-04 High-intent action → qualification → human or automated route
summary: Decide, after a commercially serious act, whether the next step needs a person's judgement or can continue automatically - and resolve what already exists before creating anything.

distinctFrom.because: ACQ-05 reacts to a qualification state that has already changed. This one runs at the moment of the act, before any state has been decided, and its output is a routing decision rather than a state.

title: ACQ-05 Qualification state change → route, re-route or exit
summary: Treat qualification as a reversible state whose routing depends on why it changed, rather than a label applied once and trusted afterwards.

distinctFrom.because: ACQ-10 handles a decision the other side made. This handles a decision our own qualification made, which can be reversed by new information without anyone changing their mind.

title: ACQ-06 Dynamic eligibility → eligible or ineligible → consequence
summary: Re-decide eligibility as the underlying data changes, and separate what it forbids next from what it does not undo.

distinctFrom.because: Qualification asks whether we want this relationship. Eligibility asks whether the rules permit a specific action, which can flip repeatedly while qualification never moves.

title: ACQ-07 Intent decay → de-prioritise → cooldown or exit
summary: Let a recorded high-intent state expire when the evidence behind it goes stale, instead of pursuing someone on the strength of something they did once.

distinctFrom.because: Nobody said no here. Decay is the absence of continuing evidence, and it must not be recorded as a decision the person never made.

title: ACQ-08 Commercial destination reached → acquisition suppression → lifecycle handoff
summary: Make acquisition give up ownership the moment the outcome it existed to cause is recorded, and stop what it has already queued.

distinctFrom.because: Escalation re-ranks journeys that are all still live. This one ends a class of them, because the objective they shared has been met.

title: ACQ-09 Researching lead → bounded education → progress or sunset
summary: Give a legitimate but not-yet-ready lead a window of useful education that ends whether or not it worked.

distinctFrom.because: Decay retires an intent state that has gone stale. This spends a deliberately fixed window trying to advance one, and only then closes it.

title: ACQ-10 Explicit commercial decline → reason → terminal, cooldown or recycle
summary: Route a negative commercial outcome by its cause rather than filing every one of them under lost.

distinctFrom.because: Someone decided something here. Where the recorded reason turns out to be silence rather than a decision, this journey hands it to decay instead of treating it as one.

title: ACT-11 New entry → onboarding route → appropriate path
summary: Choose the onboarding path from the work actually required to reach value, before any of that work starts.

distinctFrom.because: This routes on the work required, which is usually readable from the account itself. ACT-19 fires only where a named role or use-case is missing and the answer would change the path.

title: ACT-12 Onboarding progress → next best setup step → activation
summary: Advance onboarding from the state the setup record actually reports, one useful step at a time, until activation or the window ends.

title: ACT-13 Missing activation requirement → resolve blocker → resume
summary: Aim the whole journey at one named missing thing, and resume onboarding once it exists.

distinctFrom.because: Here the obstacle has a name and resolving it is the whole job. ACT-14 is for the case where nothing specific is missing and the person is still not getting anywhere.

title: ACT-14 Struggling user detection → proactive assistance → recovery or exit
summary: Offer help to someone who is visibly trying and not getting anywhere, and stop asking once they have answered.

distinctFrom.because: ACT-13 has a named requirement to clear. Here the evidence is effort without progress and no single thing to point at, which is why the offer is help rather than an instruction.

title: ACT-15 First value milestone → recognition → next meaningful action
summary: Mark the moment the product first did something real for this person, and point at whatever naturally follows from it.

distinctFrom.because: The same event can drive both, and they do opposite work. ACT-16 stops what onboarding still had queued; this one speaks to the person about what they just did.

title: ACT-16 Activation achieved → stop onboarding → adoption handoff
summary: Make onboarding let go the moment activation is recorded, including the messages it has already queued.

title: ACT-17 Early adoption → usage depth → habit or stable use
summary: Carry an account from having produced value once to producing it repeatedly, measured against its own use-case.

distinctFrom.because: Onboarding gets someone to value once. This is about the second, fifth and twentieth time, where the obstacle is habit rather than setup.

title: ACT-18 Adoption stall → diagnose missing value → recover or re-route
summary: Work out why value stopped recurring before doing anything about it, including the case where nothing is wrong.

distinctFrom.because: ACT-14 is pre-activation and triggered by help-seeking. This is post-activation and triggered by silence, where the most common correct answer is that nothing is wrong.

title: ACT-19 Role or use-case discovery → relevant onboarding adaptation
summary: Get the one piece of context onboarding needs to choose a path, only when not having it would actually change that path.

title: ACT-20 Dormant non-customer reactivation → return → re-qualification or exit
summary: Make one bounded attempt to restart a relationship that never became a paying one, and judge the result on what the person actually did.

distinctFrom.because: Decay retires an intent state that is no longer credible. This tries to restart a relationship that had already started, and it only applies where money never changed hands.

title: CMS-201 Business event → communication obligation → create or suppress
summary: Decide whether anyone is actually owed a message about what happened, before any message exists.

distinctFrom.because: FBK-41 decides whether it is appropriate to ask somebody for something. This decides whether a business event creates an obligation to tell somebody something - the requirement comes from the event and the rules, not from the recipient's receptiveness.

title: CMS-202 Communication obligation → resolve recipient → ready, hold or fail
summary: Establish who is actually owed this, and where they can currently be reached.

title: CMS-203 Communication purpose → permission and preference check → allow, suppress or alternate
summary: Decide whether a working destination may carry this particular message, given what it is for.

distinctFrom.because: CON-35 owns consent and permission as authoritative state, and propagates changes to it. This evaluates that state for one message's actual purpose - it can suppress a channel the recipient has permitted, and permit one they have not, where mandatory-delivery rules say so.

title: CMS-204 Channel selection → choose route → prepare message
summary: Pick the smallest set of channels that actually satisfies the obligation, and build the message for them.

title: CMS-205 Message prepared → revalidate state → send or suppress
summary: Check the message is still true immediately before it goes, and stop it if it is not.

title: CMS-206 Send attempt → accepted, failed or unknown
summary: Record what happened when the message was handed to a provider, which is not what happened to the recipient.

distinctFrom.because: This is the handover to a provider - accepted, refused or unanswered. CMS-207 is what the channel later reports about whether it reached anyone. A message can be accepted and never delivered, and the two states must be separately visible.

title: CMS-207 Delivery outcome → delivered, failed or unknown → update communication
summary: Derive the real delivery state from what the channel reports, attached to the exact attempt it concerns.

title: CMS-208 Delivery failure → classify → retry, fallback or stop
summary: Respond to the failure that actually happened, without spreading it wider than the destination it belongs to.

distinctFrom.because: OPS-124 is the generic retryable-failure and backoff mechanism. This decides what a communication failure means - whether the address is dead, whether another channel may carry this purpose, and whether the message is even still worth delivering. It uses that retry machinery rather than being it.

title: CMS-210 Communication outcome → close obligation or escalate unreachable
summary: Close the obligation against what it actually required, and escalate the ones that could not be met.

title: CON-31 Permission capture → validate scope → activate or reject
summary: Turn a permission decision into an auditable record of what exactly was authorised, rather than a flag that says yes.

distinctFrom.because: This creates authorisation. CON-32 records how someone would like authorised communication done, which is a different fact and must never be able to create this one.

title: CON-32 Preference capture → persist → personalise eligible communication
summary: Record how someone would like permitted communication done, in a store that structurally cannot become permission.

title: CON-33 Preference change → recalculate active journeys → suppress or adapt
summary: Make a preference change reach the messages already sitting in a queue, not just the profile field.

title: CON-34 Communication frequency change → recalculate cadence → apply prospectively
summary: Recalculate how often optional communication may go out, without letting that quietly reach the messages someone has to receive.

distinctFrom.because: A frequency preference changes how much rather than what, which means recalculating a cadence across classes rather than adapting individual queued actions.

title: CON-35 Consent or permission change → immediate enforcement → propagate
summary: Stop affected communication the moment permission changes, and let the distributed systems catch up afterwards.

distinctFrom.because: CON-31 creates a permission. This changes one that exists, and the difference that matters is that a change can be a withdrawal, which has to be enforced before it has been agreed anywhere else.

title: CON-36 Channel contactability change → recalculate reachability → route or suppress
summary: Track whether a channel can reach someone, as a state entirely separate from whether it may, and keep each destination's route health separately so future sending routes around what is broken.

distinctFrom.because: One is about capability and the other about authorisation. They are stored separately precisely so that a bounce can never look like an opt-out.

title: CON-38 Communication suppression → reason → release or persist
summary: Make every reason something is not being sent an explicit, scoped, releasable state rather than an absence.

distinctFrom.because: A cooldown is one reason among the nine this journey holds. It has its own journey because its release is time-based and its scope is deliberately partial, which the general mechanism does not assume.

title: CON-39 Communication cooldown → hold optional messaging → re-evaluate
summary: Reduce optional communication pressure for a while, without touching permission and without covering more than it needs to.

title: CON-40 Permission conflict → fail-safe state → reconcile → restore
summary: Hold optional communication closed while two systems disagree about permission, and reconcile on evidence rather than on whichever value allows more.

distinctFrom.because: CON-35 propagates a state it knows to be right. This one runs when nobody knows which state is right, which is why it starts by closing rather than by deciding.

title: CTL-231 Ownership assignment → validate authority → assign or reject
summary: Establish an accountable controller for an entity, by an explicit act rather than by inference.

distinctFrom.because: ACC-71 qualifies an entitlement - what somebody may do. This establishes who is accountable for the entity itself. An administrator can hold every entitlement the owner holds and still not be the party answerable for it.

title: CTL-232 Ownership transfer request → validate → pending acceptance or reject
summary: Propose a future controller without disturbing the one the entity currently has.

distinctFrom.because: This validates that a transfer may be proposed at all. CTL-233 validates that it is still valid when somebody finally accepts it, which is a different question asked against a different state of the world.

title: CTL-233 Ownership transfer acceptance → revalidate → execute or expire
summary: Check that a transfer accepted today is still the transfer that was proposed.

title: CTL-234 Ownership cutover → assign new owner → reconcile old owner
summary: Move control from one party to another without the entity being uncontrolled in between.

distinctFrom.because: TRM-104 transfers a primary relationship and its dependencies during account consolidation. This is the ownership control boundary specifically - establishing an accountable controller before removing the previous one, which is a sequencing requirement rather than a dependency migration.

title: CTL-235 Delegation request → define scope → grant or reject
summary: Let somebody act on an owner's behalf, inside a boundary, without moving anything.

distinctFrom.because: A transfer moves accountability permanently to somebody else. A delegation lends bounded authority while the owner stays the owner, stays accountable, and can revoke it. Treating one as the other moves control nobody moved.

title: CTL-236 Temporary delegation → expire → revoke, extend or restore
summary: End borrowed authority at its boundary, checking first that the boundary still belongs to a delegation that exists.

title: CTL-237 Delegation revoked → remove delegated authority → preserve independent access
summary: Take back exactly what was lent, and nothing the delegate had of their own.

distinctFrom.because: ACC-74 handles entitlement loss for a party losing rights. This decides which of a party's rights were borrowed and which were their own - and its whole difficulty is that removing the wrong set locks somebody out of an account they independently administer.

title: CTL-238 Owner unavailable or invalid → protect entity → recover ownership
summary: Hold an entity safely when its owner cannot act, without handing it to whoever is nearest.

title: DAT-221 Data intake → identify format → parse or reject
summary: Get an incoming dataset into a stable readable form, without touching anything real while doing it.

title: DAT-222 Parsed data → validate schema and semantics → accept, reject or quarantine
summary: Establish that the data is valid for the target it is going into, record by record where that is meaningful.

title: DAT-223 Valid data → preview and impact analysis → confirm or hold
summary: Show what the mutation would actually do, so an approval attaches to that rather than to a filename.

title: DAT-224 Import execution → apply idempotently → complete, partial or fail
summary: Apply a fixed validated change set to production state, keeping every record's outcome.

distinctFrom.because: OPS-121 runs a unit of async work and reports whether it finished. This mutates production data from a validated set, so its outcomes are per-record rather than per-job and its defining requirement is that re-running it does not create a second copy of everything that already worked.

title: DAT-225 Partial import → isolate failed scope → correct → resume
summary: Fix only what did not land, without touching the records that already did.

distinctFrom.because: OPS-126 preserves completed work in a composite processing job and retries the failed part. This works at record grain against production data, where a retry can create a duplicate row, a correction can silently alter a record that was already right, and the unresolved scope has to stay linked to the original import.

title: DAT-226 Migration plan → map source to target → validate readiness
summary: Prove the target can carry the source's meaning before anything is moved.

distinctFrom.because: This proves the mapping can work. DAT-227 runs it and checks what actually arrived. A mapping that passes design review can still lose relationships at volume, and a mapping that never existed cannot be discovered mid-run.

title: DAT-227 Migration execute → copy and transform → verify population
summary: Move the population and then prove the result still means what the source meant.

distinctFrom.because: This produces a verified target population. DAT-228 changes which system answers - a separate act, with live traffic depending on it, and its own recovery path.

title: DAT-228 Cutover → switch authority → observe → stabilize or roll back
summary: Change which system is authoritative, once, with a way back that was defined before it was needed.

title: DAT-229 Historical backfill → scope window → apply without replaying stale actions
summary: Repair a gap in the record without re-enacting the things those events would have caused.

distinctFrom.because: INT-118 backfills what an integration missed while it was disconnected, and reconciles against a partner system. This repairs a historical gap from any source, and its defining problem is suppressing the real-time side effects those events would have triggered - a question a reconnect backfill answers differently.

title: DAT-230 Data transformation error → reconcile → correct, roll forward or roll back
summary: Undo the wrong mutation without undoing the right things that happened after it.

title: DEC-181 Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
summary: Establish that authorized judgment is genuinely required, and open a case whose scope is stated.

distinctFrom.because: A submission journey qualifies something that arrived. This exists only where a deterministic rule cannot produce the answer and an authorized person must - which is why its first substantive check is whether policy could already decide it.

title: DEC-182 Decision case → assign reviewer → accept, reassign or escalate
summary: Put the case in front of someone who is actually authorized to decide it, and make that ownership explicit.

distinctFrom.because: This moves ownership within the same authority level, because someone is unavailable, conflicted or too slow. Escalation moves it to a different or higher authority, because the current level cannot decide the question at all.

OWN-51 routes work to whoever can do it. This routes a decision to whoever is authorized to make it - availability is not eligibility here, and a decision made by an unauthorized reviewer looks valid and is void.

title: DEC-183 Review started → evaluate evidence → decide or request more information
summary: Turn sufficient evidence into an authorized decision, within the scope the reviewer actually holds.

distinctFrom.because: IDN-84 recovers from a verification that failed - a mechanical outcome with retry and remediation routes. This is a person exercising judgment against criteria, where the failure mode is deciding outside your authority rather than failing a check.

title: DEC-184 More information required → collect → revalidate → resume review
summary: Pause a decision for the fact it is actually missing, without losing the review already done.

distinctFrom.because: FBK-49 resolves missing data blocking a process generally. This is evidence a named reviewer needs to answer a specific open question - it is scoped by the decision rather than by the record, and it ends by resuming a review rather than by unblocking a pipeline.

title: DEC-185 Approval decision → revalidate target → execute, hold or invalidate
summary: Carry an authorization into execution, having checked it still applies to what it was granted against.

distinctFrom.because: This carries a whole authorized scope into execution. DEC-187 exists because a partitioned scope raises a separate problem - which parts may proceed, and whether the action can be half-done at all.

title: DEC-186 Rejection decision → record reason → remediate, close or reapply
summary: Treat a refusal as the business outcome it is, and say what if anything the requester can do next.

distinctFrom.because: This is the first decision's rejection outcome. FBK-47 is the appeal or reconsideration lifecycle, which exists only where policy grants that right - and this journey hands to it rather than performing it.

OWN-59 handles an approval rejected inside a work-ownership flow and asks whether a revision may be resubmitted. This is the decision-case rejection with its full reason taxonomy, and its three separate exits: correctable, reapplicable, and appealable.

title: DEC-187 Partial approval → split scope → execute approved, resolve remaining
summary: Make the authorized and unauthorized halves of one request explicit, so only the first can move.

distinctFrom.because: DEC-185 executes an authorization whose scope is whole. This has to partition a scope first, and then answer a question DEC-185 never faces: whether the action can be half-done at all.

title: DEC-188 Approval validity or expiry → revalidate → use, expire or renew review
summary: Answer, at the moment of use, whether an approval is still one - in time, in context and in count.

title: DEC-189 Decision escalation → higher authority → decide, return or reassign
summary: Move a case to an authority that can actually resolve it, carrying the work already done and predetermining nothing.

distinctFrom.because: DEC-182 moves ownership at the same authority level because someone cannot take it. This moves the case to a different or higher authority because the current level cannot decide the question at all.
OWN-55 escalates responsibility for work that is stuck. This escalates decision authority specifically - the case is not stuck, it is in front of someone who is not permitted to answer it.

title: DEC-190 Decision superseded or reopened → revalidate → continue or new decision
summary: Let a decision be reconsidered without any part of the original being rewritten.

distinctFrom.because: OWN-58 asks whether a material change after approval needs re-approval, inside a work-ownership flow. This owns the decision record's history: what supersedes what, what was already executed, and what a new decision does not undo.

title: DOC-211 Document requirement → determine artifact → create, reuse or waive
summary: Decide whether a new artifact is genuinely needed, or whether one already exists that answers the requirement.

distinctFrom.because: RSK-195 owns the compliance requirement itself - whether an obligation is met. This owns the artifact lifecycle a requirement may need: which document, generated how, issued when, signed by whom. A compliance requirement can be satisfied without any document, and most documents exist for reasons that are not compliance.

title: DOC-212 Document draft → populate → validate → ready or blocked
summary: Build the contents from authoritative sources and prove they are complete before anything is issued.

title: DOC-213 Ready document → issue → immutable issued version
summary: Freeze the artifact at a version that can be identified, referenced and never quietly changed.

title: DOC-214 Document distribution → send or provide access → confirm or fail
summary: Get a specific issued version to the party who should have it, without either fact touching the other.

title: DOC-215 Signature request → await signatures → signed, declined or expired
summary: Collect the required signatures against one exact version, and know when they are actually all there.

distinctFrom.because: DEC-183 is somebody exercising judgment against criteria. This is collecting authorized marks against a fixed artifact - nobody is deciding anything on the merits, and its failure modes are version binding, incomplete sets and expiry rather than authority to conclude.

title: DOC-216 Signed document → validate completion → effective or pending condition
summary: Establish when a document actually starts doing something, which is not when it was signed.

distinctFrom.because: SUB-161 makes a continuing relationship active. This makes a document effective, which may be what triggers that - but a document can be effective without creating a relationship, and a relationship can activate without any document.

title: DOC-217 Document change → new version or amendment → supersede prospectively
summary: Change an issued artifact by creating a successor, leaving what it replaces exactly as it was.

title: DOC-218 Document expiry → revalidate requirement → renew, replace or close
summary: End future reliance on a time-limited artifact, and stop only what genuinely needs it to be current.

distinctFrom.because: Expiry is time running out on terms the document itself set. Revocation is an authority withdrawing it. Nobody decided the first, somebody decided the second, and they carry different consequences for what was relied on meanwhile.

title: DOC-219 Document revocation or withdrawal → stop future reliance → reconcile
summary: Withdraw an artifact by an authority's decision, exactly as far as that decision reaches.

distinctFrom.because: An amendment replaces a document with a successor that carries the same purpose forward. Revocation withdraws it with nothing behind it - there may be no successor, and the reason is a decision rather than a change of terms.

title: DOC-220 Document or record conflict → determine authoritative version → reconcile
summary: Work out which version actually governs, and explain the conflict rather than deleting it.

distinctFrom.because: A generic sync conflict asks which record is newer. This asks which version is authoritative, which turns on issuance authority, lineage and effective semantics - and it must additionally establish which version each signature actually binds to, a question recency cannot answer.

title: FBK-41 Feedback eligibility → ask, suppress or delay
summary: Decide whether asking is appropriate at all, and hold the gap between asking and hearing back as a real state.

distinctFrom.because: This ends when a request has been made or refused. FBK-43 begins only if something actually comes back, and most requests do not produce one.

title: FBK-42 Advocacy eligibility → ask, delay or suppress
summary: Ask someone to vouch for us only where the relationship has actually earned it, and keep public reuse a separate permission.

distinctFrom.because: FBK-45 reacts to one positive signal arriving. This weighs the accumulated relationship and decides whether it can carry a request - most positive signals do not reach it.

title: FBK-43 Feedback received → classify → route → close the loop
summary: Get feedback to the process that can act on it, and keep the record open until anything promised in return has actually happened.

title: FBK-44 Negative feedback → issue check → resolve, acknowledge or escalate
summary: Find out whether an unresolved obligation actually exists before anything that looks like recovery starts.

distinctFrom.because: RET-26 starts from a recorded failure and asks what response is owed. This starts from someone's account of an experience and asks whether a failure exists at all - which most often it does not.

title: FBK-45 Positive feedback → recognition → advocacy opportunity
summary: Record a good experience as evidence and acknowledge it, without turning the person into an advocate by arithmetic.

title: FBK-46 Complaint or issue created → ownership → resolution → confirmation
summary: Hold an actionable issue as an open obligation with a named owner until both the fix and the closure condition are satisfied.

title: FBK-47 Appeal or dispute → evidence review → uphold, reverse or modify
summary: Review a decision that has already been made, without erasing it while the review is running.

distinctFrom.because: An issue is something that went wrong. An appeal contests something we did on purpose, which means the subject under review is our own decision and it has to remain intact to be reviewable.

title: FBK-48 Declared need or preference signal → persist → recalculate relevant experience
summary: Let something a person has told us about their situation reach the decisions that actually depend on it, and nothing else.

distinctFrom.because: CON-32 records how someone wants to be communicated with. This records what they are trying to achieve, which shapes product and journey decisions rather than message delivery.

title: FBK-49 Missing critical data → request or resolve → resume
summary: Treat a genuinely blocking data gap as a named dependency, and keep it distinct from wanting to know more about someone.

distinctFrom.because: ACT-13 is scoped to activation specifically and owns resuming onboarding. This applies to any named process, most of which have nothing to do with onboarding.

title: FBK-50 Relationship signal → evidence accumulation → state reassessment
summary: Accumulate signals as dated evidence, and let a relationship label exist only where a policy defined what it means.

distinctFrom.because: RET-21 recalculates engagement from behaviour on a defined cadence. This accumulates heterogeneous signals - feedback, outcomes, friction, contributions - and only reassesses a state where the evidence justifies it.

title: FIN-131 Financial obligation created → due → satisfied or outstanding
summary: Hold what is owed as its own state, independent of any attempt to pay it and of anything sent about it.

distinctFrom.because: An attempt is one try at discharging an obligation. It can fail without the obligation changing at all, which is exactly why they are two entities.

title: FIN-132 Payment initiated → pending → success, failure or unknown
summary: Keep initiating a payment and knowing what happened to it as separate states, with a third state for not knowing.

distinctFrom.because: INT-114 is the generic shape of an external operation. This carries financial semantics the generic version has no room for: an obligation behind it, an authorization that is not money, and an unknown state whose safe response is to investigate rather than retry.

title: FIN-133 Payment authorization → capture → settle or release
summary: Model the actual commitment of funds, where reserving, taking and receiving are three different things.

title: FIN-134 Payment failure → classify → recover, alternate or exit
summary: Respond to the reason a payment actually failed, and keep the obligation alive while doing it.

distinctFrom.because: OPS-124 is a generic technical retry against a transient fault. This makes a business recovery decision: what to ask the customer for, whether an alternative route exists, and what happens to the obligation if none of it works.

title: FIN-135 Payment unknown → reconcile → confirm success or failure
summary: Find out what actually happened to a payment whose outcome we lost sight of, before anything is charged again.

distinctFrom.because: Here one attempt's outcome is unknown and the provider can answer it. FIN-140 is where several records exist and disagree, which needs comparison and correction rather than a question.

title: FIN-136 Financial obligation satisfied → reconcile balance → release dependent state
summary: Apply a financial event to an obligation exactly once, and release only what actually depended on that obligation.

title: FIN-137 Refund request → eligibility → approve, reject or review
summary: Turn a refund request into an authorised decision, without money moving on the request itself.

distinctFrom.because: Approving a refund authorises the movement. FIN-138 performs it and confirms the money arrived, which fails independently and more often than the decision does.

title: FIN-138 Refund approved → execute → confirm or reconcile
summary: Move the money and confirm it arrived, keeping that separate from having decided it should.

title: FIN-139 Financial dispute or chargeback → evidence → decision → reconcile
summary: Run a transaction-level dispute through the authority that decides it, without treating the claim as a finding.

distinctFrom.because: FBK-47 reviews a decision we made, under our own process. A chargeback is adjudicated by a card scheme or a regulator with power to move funds regardless of what we conclude, and missing its deadline decides it against us whatever the evidence says.

title: FIN-140 Financial reconciliation → detect mismatch → correct or escalate
summary: Restore financial consistency by explaining the difference and adjusting it, never by editing the record that is inconvenient.

distinctFrom.because: FIN-135 has one attempt and no answer, and the provider can supply one. Here every system has an answer and they disagree, which needs comparison, an authority rule and an explicit adjustment.

title: FUL-141 Fulfillment request → validate → accept, reject or hold
summary: Decide whether we are taking responsibility for delivering something, as a state distinct from having been asked.

distinctFrom.because: FIN-131 creates an obligation to pay. This creates an obligation to deliver. They arise from the same event and fail independently - a paid order can be unfulfillable, and a delivered one can go unpaid.

title: FUL-142 Accepted fulfillment → availability check → allocate, backorder or reject
summary: Establish whether the resources to satisfy an accepted obligation actually exist, in the scope and window that would serve it.

distinctFrom.because: This asks whether something exists. FUL-143 claims it. Between the two, someone else can take it - which is why the reading and the claim are separate steps and the claim is the one that counts.

title: FUL-143 Resource allocation → reserve → confirm, release or reallocate
summary: Bind specific capacity to one obligation until it is consumed or deliberately let go.

title: FUL-144 Fulfillment execution → progress → complete, partial or fail
summary: Track what the obligation's scope actually reaches, rather than what an internal step reported.

distinctFrom.because: OPS-130 asks whether a technical job produced the state it claimed. This runs the operational execution of a real delivery obligation, where the outcome is measured in scope satisfied rather than in a state existing.

title: FUL-145 Fulfillment exception → diagnose → recover, substitute or fail
summary: Change only the part of an obligation the operational problem actually touches.

distinctFrom.because: An exception is something going wrong with the ability to fulfill. A delay is the same obligation arriving later. Where an exception only changes timing, it hands to FUL-146 rather than resolving as one.

title: FUL-146 Fulfillment delay → recalculate commitment → continue, reschedule or escalate
summary: Hold lateness as its own state, with the original commitment intact behind whatever the new estimate is.

title: FUL-147 Dispatch or handoff → track → delivered, failed or unknown
summary: Transfer execution to whoever performs the delivery while the obligation stays ours and stays open.

distinctFrom.because: INT-114 is the generic shape of an external operation. This carries delivery semantics that shape has no room for: a recipient who may refuse, an attempt that is not an outcome, and intermediate tracking updates that look like results and are not.

title: FUL-148 Delivery attempt failed → reason → retry, correct, alternate or return
summary: Recover a failed delivery according to why it failed, within a bounded number of attempts.

title: FUL-149 Delivery confirmation → acceptance or issue window → finalize
summary: Separate arriving from being agreed to have arrived correctly, wherever that difference has business meaning.

title: FUL-150 Fulfillment cancellation → stop future work → release resources → reconcile
summary: Stop what remains of an obligation while keeping everything that already happened.

distinctFrom.because: Stopping a delivery and returning money are different decisions with different authority. Coupling them either refunds what was delivered or delivers what was refunded, and this journey hands the financial question to the lifecycle that owns it.

title: IDN-81 Identity claim → evidence → verified, rejected or more evidence
summary: Establish confidence in one specific identity claim, bound to the evidence that established it.

distinctFrom.because: Verification asks whether a claim is true. Authentication asks whether whoever is present right now controls it. A verified claim from last year says nothing about who is at the keyboard.

title: IDN-82 Verification requirement → collect evidence → resume blocked process
summary: Hold a verification dependency as its own state, blocking only the process that needs it and releasing it only after everything else is rechecked.

distinctFrom.because: FBK-49 is missing data - a value we do not hold. This is missing confidence - we may hold the value and have not established that it is true. The routes to resolving them share nothing.

title: IDN-83 Document submitted → validate → accept, reject or replace
summary: Keep uploading a document and satisfying a requirement as separate facts, and keep an acceptance bound to the requirement it was assessed against.

title: IDN-84 Verification failure → reason → retry, remediate, review or exit
summary: Route a failed verification by why it failed, and keep our own failures out of the customer's verification record.

title: IDN-85 Authentication challenge → authenticate, step up or deny
summary: Establish that whoever is present controls the required identity, at the assurance the context demands.

distinctFrom.because: This establishes who is present. ACC-75 decides what they may do. A successful authentication is an input to that decision and never a substitute for it.

title: IDN-86 Step-up requirement → stronger authentication → resume or deny
summary: Raise identity assurance for a sensitive action, then check the action is still authorised before it runs.

title: IDN-87 Authentication failure pattern → security check → recover or restrict
summary: Tell an ordinary forgotten password apart from an account under attack, without converting the first into the second.

distinctFrom.because: This weighs whether failures mean anything. IDN-90 starts from a material compromise signal and contains first. The route between them exists, and it is deliberately a decision rather than a default.

title: IDN-88 Account recovery request → prove control → restore secure access
summary: Give someone a way back into an account they can no longer authenticate to, without that route being weaker than the one it replaces.

distinctFrom.because: Verification establishes that a claim is true. Recovery establishes that this requester is entitled to regain control of a specific account, which a true claim about their identity does not by itself demonstrate.

title: IDN-89 Identity attribute change → verify if required → update → propagate
summary: Change an identity attribute safely, and reconcile everything that depended on the old value independently rather than by inheritance.

title: IDN-90 Suspected account compromise → contain → verify → recover or clear
summary: Limit the damage a possible compromise could do while the question is still open, and reach a conclusion that can go either way.

distinctFrom.because: Suspension restricts for a stated business reason and expects to be resolved by that reason going away. This restricts on incomplete evidence about an adversary, which is why it opens an investigation rather than a review.

title: INC-251 Correlated failure detection → incident candidate → confirm or reject
summary: Establish whether several failures actually share a cause, before treating them as one thing.

distinctFrom.because: RSK-192 assesses risk evidence about one actor or transaction. This asks whether failures across many unrelated entities plausibly share an operational cause - a question about the system rather than about anybody using it.

title: INC-252 Incident confirmed → determine severity and blast radius → assign command
summary: Establish what is actually affected, how badly, and who is running the response.

title: INC-253 Incident → contain and mitigate → preserve critical operations
summary: Reduce the damage now, without pretending the cause has been dealt with.

distinctFrom.because: Mitigation reduces impact while the cause remains. INC-256 acts on the cause and asks whether the service actually came back. A system can be fully mitigated and entirely unfixed, and reporting the first as the second stops the second happening.

title: INC-254 Incident communication → identify affected cohort → inform, update or close
summary: Tell the people actually affected something true and useful, through the mechanism that already owns delivery.

title: INC-255 Root cause investigation → hypothesis → confirm or reject → corrective action
summary: Find the thing that actually explains the incident, rather than the thing that was nearest to it.

title: INC-256 Recovery action → restore service → verify or continue
summary: Act on the cause and then check the affected population, not the command's return code.

title: INC-257 Service restored → observation window → stable or relapse
summary: Hold the incident open long enough to know the recovery held.

distinctFrom.because: RET-27 buffers one relationship's recovery signal before concluding the relationship is healthy. This applies the same principle to a shared operational failure - same discipline, different entity, and here a relapse returns a population to an incident rather than a person to a risk state.

title: INC-258 Incident resolution → close operational response → preserve residual cases
summary: Close the shared failure without closing the individual problems it caused.

title: INC-259 Post-incident review → learn → corrective work → verify
summary: Turn what the incident showed into work somebody owns and somebody checks.

title: INC-260 Incident pattern recurrence → detect systemic weakness → escalate prevention
summary: Notice when the same weakness keeps producing incidents, and stop treating each one as new.

distinctFrom.because: INC-251 correlates failures happening now into one incident. This compares incidents across time to ask whether the same systemic weakness keeps producing them - a question about the prevention strategy rather than about any one response.

title: INT-111 Integration connection → authenticate → validate → activate
summary: Make an integration active only once it has been proven to do the thing it exists for, rather than once a credential has been saved.

distinctFrom.because: This establishes that an integration works at all. INT-113 handles one that worked and has started to stop, which is a question about evidence over a window rather than about setup.

title: INT-112 Integration credential or authorization change → revalidate → continue or degrade
summary: Recheck what an integration can still do whenever its authorization changes, rather than assuming valid credentials mean unchanged access.

title: INT-113 Integration health degradation → diagnose → recover, degrade or escalate
summary: Scope a deteriorating integration to what is actually failing, and let recovery be established by evidence rather than by a metric returning to normal.

title: INT-114 External request → pending outcome → confirm, fail or unknown
summary: Keep submitting an external operation and completing one as separate states, and let an unknown outcome stay unknown.

distinctFrom.because: This owns the operation from submission until an outcome exists. INT-115 owns what happens to local state once one does, and most operations pass through both.

title: INT-115 External outcome → local state reconciliation → apply or investigate
summary: Apply an external outcome to local state only after establishing that it belongs here, has not already been applied, and still describes what is true.

title: INT-116 Integration failure → stop unsafe operations → diagnose → restore
summary: Stop sending into an integration that cannot work, while keeping enough state to recover without repeating anything the provider may already have done.

distinctFrom.because: Degradation is an integration working badly and still working. This is one that cannot be relied on to work at all, which changes what is safe to send rather than how much.

title: INT-117 Integration failure → queue or hold work → recover → controlled resume
summary: Keep work that a failed integration blocked, but only where it can later be revalidated and safely resumed.

distinctFrom.because: This applies only where the integration has genuinely failed. An integration that is merely slow or backlogged is still working, and queueing more against it adds to the backlog that is already the problem - that case is a separate canonical problem and is deliberately not handled here.

title: INT-118 Integration reconnect → backfill → deduplicate → reconcile
summary: Close the gap an outage left in what we know, without recreating everything that would have happened if the events had arrived on time.

title: INT-119 Synchronization conflict → determine authority → reconcile or hold
summary: Settle a cross-system disagreement using an explicit authority rule, and hold rather than guess where none exists.

distinctFrom.because: CON-40 is a permission conflict and fails closed by suppressing communication. This is a general data conflict, where the safe state is holding the mutation rather than stopping outbound messaging.

title: INT-120 External dependency unavailable → degrade capability → alternate or recover
summary: Lose only the capability that actually depends on an unavailable provider, and keep every uncertain outcome uncertain.

distinctFrom.because: INT-116 is about our integration to a provider failing. This is about the provider itself being unavailable, where an alternate path may exist and the question is what our product can still do.

title: OPS-121 Work accepted → queue → process → complete or fail
summary: Give asynchronous work explicit states so that acknowledging it, holding it, running it and finishing it are never read as the same event.

distinctFrom.because: This ends when the job reports an outcome. OPS-130 begins there and asks whether the business state the job existed to create actually appeared, which is a separate question with its own answer.

title: OPS-122 Queue lag → measure → prioritise, scale or degrade
summary: Respond to a queue that cannot keep up, measured by how old the unfinished work is rather than by how much of it there is.

distinctFrom.because: INT-117 holds work because an integration has failed and cannot accept it. Here the dependency may be perfectly healthy and our own capacity is behind - queueing more against it makes the backlog worse rather than protecting anything.

title: OPS-123 Work stalled → detect lack of progress → recover, fail or escalate
summary: Distinguish work that is taking a long time from work that has stopped, and recover only where the side effects are known.

title: OPS-124 Retryable failure → backoff → retry → resolve or exhaust
summary: Repeat a transient failure within a bounded budget, only where repeating is safe and the work is still wanted.

distinctFrom.because: Retry is automated recovery while it can still work. Dead-lettering is what happens once it has run out, and it produces a human obligation rather than another attempt.

title: OPS-125 Duplicate work detected → deduplicate → reuse, suppress or reconcile
summary: Stop the same logical operation running twice, without collapsing two legitimate repeats into one.

title: OPS-126 Partial processing → preserve completed work → retry only the failed scope
summary: Recover the part of a composite operation that failed, without re-running the part that worked.

title: OPS-127 Dead-letter entry → diagnose → replay, correct or close
summary: Turn work that automation could not finish into an obligation someone owns, rather than a queue nobody reads.

distinctFrom.because: Retry is the automated stage and ends when its budget does. This begins there, and what it produces is a diagnosis and an owner rather than another attempt.

title: OPS-128 Worker or processor failure → reclaim work → resume safely
summary: Move execution responsibility off a failed worker without assuming the work failed and without letting two workers hold it.

title: OPS-129 Backlog recovery → revalidate → controlled drain → normal state
summary: Work through an accumulated backlog deliberately, discarding what has gone stale and pacing what has not.

distinctFrom.because: INT-118 repairs a gap in what we received from outside during an outage. This drains work we already hold and could not process. One is missing information; the other is unfinished work.

title: OPS-130 Technical completion → verify business outcome → finalize or reconcile
summary: Check that the state a job existed to create actually exists, wherever the job's own success is not proof of it.

title: OWN-51 Work created → routing → assignment
summary: Get new work into the smallest responsibility scope that is genuinely valid, and refuse to invent one where the policy is silent.

distinctFrom.because: This decides where the work belongs. OWN-52 decides whether the person it landed on has taken it, which is a different state and frequently a different answer.

title: OWN-52 Assignment → acceptance → active responsibility
summary: Keep proposed responsibility and accepted responsibility as different states, so work nobody has taken is visible as such.

title: OWN-53 Owner assignment → context transfer → work start
summary: Give a new owner what they need to continue an existing obligation, rather than an entity with their name on it.

distinctFrom.because: OWN-52 establishes that someone has taken responsibility. This establishes that they can actually discharge it, which fails independently and more quietly.

title: OWN-54 Ownership change → transfer obligations → continue
summary: Move responsibility for an active entity without losing anything that was already owed, without letting the clock restart, and without rewriting who did what before the change.

title: OWN-55 Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
summary: Move a blocker up to the level that can clear it, without the original owner putting the work down by raising it.

distinctFrom.because: Escalation is usually a request for a decision, not a handover. Where it does move ownership, it hands to OWN-54 to do that properly rather than doing it as a side effect.

title: OWN-56 Approval request → review → approve, reject or request changes
summary: Bind an approval to the exact version reviewed, and keep approving separate from doing.

distinctFrom.because: This is one decision by one authority. OWN-57 exists because combining several decisions requires an aggregation policy that this journey never has to consult.

title: OWN-57 Multi-party approval → aggregate required decisions → authorised or blocked
summary: Combine several genuinely independent approval decisions strictly according to the governing policy, and refuse to proceed where no policy defines how.

title: OWN-58 Material change after approval → impact check → re-approval or continue
summary: Work out whether an approval still covers what the subject has become, and re-open only the decisions whose basis stopped being true.

title: OWN-59 Approval rejected → revision eligibility → resubmit or close
summary: Keep rejection from being either a dead end by default or a retry loop, and make sure a rejected version cannot quietly execute later.

title: OWN-60 Decision authority change → revalidate pending decisions → transfer or continue
summary: Re-evaluate decisions against who is actually authorised now, without unapproving history or blindly moving what is pending.

distinctFrom.because: Ownership is who does the work; authority is who may decide. They change independently, and an approver leaving does not move a case any more than a case moving changes who may approve it.

title: REL-91 Entity relationship created → validate → activate or reject
summary: Create a link between two entities only where the relationship itself has an authoritative basis, and keep it a link rather than a consolidation.

distinctFrom.because: This establishes that a relationship exists. REL-98 defines what a link between two entities is allowed to share, which is a separate decision that many relationships answer with nothing.

SUB-161 creates a relationship that carries a term - an effective date, a renewal model and terms that can lapse. This creates a structural link between two entities, which can exist indefinitely without any of those. An employee belongs to an organisation here; the organisation's contract is created there, and the two end for different reasons on different days.

title: REL-92 Relationship change → recalculate rights and obligations → continue
summary: Recalculate exactly what depended on a relationship when it changes, and nothing else.

distinctFrom.because: This changes what the entities' structural relationship means - the type of membership, the direction of a parent-child link, the basis on which a representative acts. SUB-166 changes the authorized terms a continuing relationship runs under - the plan, the tier, the scope, the price. Someone can become a contractor instead of an employee with their subscription untouched, and move from Basic to Pro without their relationship to the organisation changing at all.

title: REL-93 Relationship end → remove future dependency → reconcile existing obligations
summary: Stop what a relationship was carrying forward without cancelling what it validly produced.

distinctFrom.because: SUB-170 ends a term: a subscription, contract, policy or membership reaches cancellation, non-renewal, expiry, termination or lapse, and what stops is what the term was granting. This ends a structural link between two entities, and what stops is what depended on the link. An employee leaving an organisation ends the link and not the organisation's contract; a contract expiring ends the term and leaves the employee where they were.

title: REL-94 Role change → authority and capability delta → apply
summary: Move what someone may do next, by the difference between two roles, without disturbing what they did under the old one.

distinctFrom.because: A role change alters what someone may do. An identity attribute change alters who they are on record. Treating a role change as an identity change rebuilds the person and loses their history.

title: REL-95 Parent state change → determine child impact → propagate selectively
summary: Let a parent's state reach only the children that genuinely depend on it, through a rule someone actually wrote.

distinctFrom.because: This propagates downward through defined dependencies. REL-96 derives upward through an aggregation policy. They are opposite directions with different rules, and neither is the inverse of the other.

title: REL-96 Child state change → recalculate aggregate parent state
summary: Derive a parent's state from its children through an explicit aggregation policy, recomputed from source rather than nudged by whichever child reported last.

title: REL-97 Duplicate entity detected → assess → keep separate, link or merge
summary: Assess whether two records are the same entity, and route the answer - without consolidating anything.

distinctFrom.because: Linking is one of the outcomes this assessment can reach. It is a separate journey because a link has its own semantics and its own sharing rules, which the assessment does not decide.

title: REL-98 Entity link → shared context → preserve independent identity
summary: Record that two entities are related and let defined context cross between them, while both remain two entities.

title: REL-99 Entity split required → create separate records → allocate history and state safely
summary: Separate what should never have been one record, or what must now be managed apart, without copying the things that do not divide.

distinctFrom.because: A link connects two records that already exist separately. A split creates that separation where it did not exist, which means deciding what each side gets - and what neither side may simply be given a copy of.

title: REL-100 Required relationship missing → orphan state → resolve or reassign
summary: Make a missing required relationship an explicit, findable state rather than a null field that active work quietly runs against.

distinctFrom.because: OWN-51 routes work that has never had an owner. This handles an entity that had a required relationship and lost it, which means inherited deadlines and obligations are already running against it.

title: REM-151 Post-completion issue → validate → remedy route
summary: Establish whether something delivered has left an obligation unresolved, and which recovery mechanism could satisfy it.

distinctFrom.because: FBK-44 starts from someone's account of an experience and asks whether any operational issue exists. This starts from a concrete problem with something already delivered and asks which recovery route would fix it - the obligation is known to exist and the question is what satisfies it.

title: REM-152 Return request → eligibility → authorize, reject or review
summary: Decide whether something may enter a return process, as a decision separate from whether money is owed.

distinctFrom.because: This grants permission for a resource to come back. REM-153 tracks whether it actually does, which fails independently and often.

title: REM-153 Return authorized → in transit, received, lost or expired
summary: Track whether an authorised return actually comes back, and hold the states where it might not have.

title: REM-154 Returned item or deliverable → inspect → accept, reject or partial
summary: Judge what came back against the conditions it was authorised under, keeping receipt and acceptance apart.

title: REM-155 Replacement decision → allocate → fulfill → confirm
summary: Deliver a second time against the same promise, tied to the defect it exists to resolve.

distinctFrom.because: FUL-144 executes an original fulfillment obligation. This creates a second one whose entire purpose is to resolve a specific defect in the first, which changes whether it is charged for and what it has to be verified against.

title: REM-156 Reperformance or correction → execute → verify corrected outcome
summary: Produce the outcome that should have been produced, while the record still shows that the first one was wrong.

distinctFrom.because: A replacement sends a different instance of the thing. A correction fixes the instance that exists, or performs the service again - which is why it has no allocation question and does have an original outcome that must not be overwritten.

title: REM-157 Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
summary: Choose the remedy that would actually satisfy the unresolved obligation, from the ones that genuinely exist.

distinctFrom.because: This decides which remedy applies. FIN-137 runs only if that decision is a refund, and then decides whether the refund is owed - a separate eligibility with separate rules.

title: REM-158 Remedy execution → verify outcome → close or continue recovery
summary: Check that the remedy actually satisfied the obligation, rather than that it was carried out.

distinctFrom.because: FBK-46 owns an issue's ownership and closure lifecycle. This verifies that a specific chosen remedy produced its intended business outcome - a narrower question, and one that can fail while the case is being managed perfectly well.

title: REM-159 Compensation decision → eligibility → grant or reject → deliver
summary: Decide separately whether impact warrants something beyond fixing the problem, and confirm it actually arrived.

distinctFrom.because: REM-157 chooses what satisfies the obligation. This decides whether the impact of the failure warrants something beyond that. A credit does not deliver the thing that was owed, and treating it as the remedy leaves someone holding money and the same broken outcome.

title: REM-160 Post-remedy reopen → validate recurrence → continue or new issue
summary: Tell a recurrence of the same problem apart from a new one, and from a remedy that never actually finished.

title: RET-21 Engagement state change → reclassify → appropriate lifecycle
summary: Hold engagement as a state that moves in both directions, and decide separately whether a movement is worth acting on.

distinctFrom.because: This reacts to a state that has already been recalculated. RET-22 reacts to one specific expected thing not happening, which may or may not move the state at all.

title: RET-22 Expected usage miss → context check → observe or intervene
summary: Read a missed usage expectation as evidence only where an expectation genuinely existed, and only where something else corroborates it.

title: RET-23 Health deterioration → diagnose cause → recovery route
summary: Send a deteriorating relationship to the mechanism that is actually breaking it, and never to a generic retention campaign in its place.

distinctFrom.because: This asks what is wrong. RET-24 asks how much is wrong and how hard to push back, and it can run on a relationship whose cause is already known and being fixed.

title: RET-24 Churn risk escalation → evidence → intervention priority
summary: Decide how hard to push back on a relationship at risk, in proportion to how much independent evidence there actually is.

title: RET-26 Negative experience → recovery eligibility → appropriate response
summary: Match the response to what actually failed, whether it is fixed, and whether a remedy is genuinely owed.

title: RET-27 Recovery signal → observation buffer → stable or relapse
summary: Keep the distance between a good sign and an actual recovery, so a relapse is still being watched for when it happens.

distinctFrom.because: An improving engagement state is one input to this. RET-21 updates a state; this decides whether an improvement should be believed yet, which is a different question with a waiting period in it.

title: RET-28 Cancellation intent → understand state → save or proceed
summary: Treat stated intent to leave as a decision point where a genuinely relevant alternative may be offered, and never as an obstacle course.

distinctFrom.because: This runs while the decision is still reversible and the person is still deciding. RET-29 runs after it is made, and the two must never share an event.

title: RET-29 Cancellation completed → stop retention → resolve remaining relationship
summary: End retention ownership the moment cancellation is real, and manage what is still outstanding without pretending the relationship is either fully over or still winnable.

title: RET-30 Retention intervention → outcome → suppress, escalate or exit
summary: Close a retention attempt on what actually happened to the relationship, and stop the same offer being made twice.

distinctFrom.because: This asks whether the intervention worked. RET-27 asks whether the improvement lasts, and takes over once this one has a positive answer.

title: RLT-241 Change candidate → eligibility → ready or blocked
summary: Decide which targets a change may reach at all, before anyone starts preparing any of them.

distinctFrom.because: This asks whether a target may take the change. RLT-242 gets it into a state where it can. Ineligible and unprepared are different problems with different owners - one is a decision, the other is work.

title: RLT-242 Change preparation → resolve dependencies → ready or hold
summary: Get an eligible target into a state where the change can actually be applied to it.

title: RLT-243 Change scheduled → wait → revalidate → execute or cancel
summary: Check, at the moment of execution, that the change scheduled earlier is still the right one for this target.

title: RLT-244 Change execution → apply → verify, fail or unknown
summary: Establish that the target actually ended up in the state the change intended, rather than that a command was accepted.

distinctFrom.because: RLT-243 decides whether to proceed. This performs the change and establishes what state the target actually reached, which is where the accepted-applied-verified distinction lives.

title: RLT-245 Staged rollout → pilot cohort → health gate → expand or hold
summary: Widen a change only when the targets that already took it show it is safe to widen.

distinctFrom.because: This is population progression - whether the next cohort may begin. RLT-249 is one target that could not take the change while the rollout is otherwise fine. Merging them turns every unreachable device into a reason to stop, or every real regression into a target exception.

title: RLT-246 Rollout pause → freeze expansion → diagnose → resume, roll back or end
summary: Stop the change spreading while the question of what to do about it is still open.

title: RLT-247 Change failure threshold → rollback decision → execute or forward recover
summary: Decide whether going back is actually safer than going on, before anyone starts going back.

distinctFrom.because: This chooses the recovery. RLT-248 performs a rollback and verifies it. Choosing wrong here is irreversible in the other direction - a rollback across a migrated schema cannot be undone by rolling forward again.

title: RLT-248 Rollback execution → restore → verify stability
summary: Return the affected targets to a known-good state and prove that they actually work there.

title: RLT-249 Individual target change failure → retry, isolate or remediate
summary: Recover one target that could not take the change, and notice when it stops being one target.

distinctFrom.because: RLT-245 governs whether the population progresses. This governs one target that fell out of it. One unreachable device is not a broken release, and treating it as one stops a rollout that was working.

title: RLT-250 Change completed → observe → close, reopen or deprecate previous version
summary: Wait long enough to know the change held, and keep what a recovery would need until it clearly does not.

title: RSK-191 Policy check → evaluate → pass, block or review
summary: Decide whether a specific action is permitted under the rules that actually govern it, at the version that actually applies.

distinctFrom.because: This applies rules. DEC-181 opens a workflow for judgment where no rule produces the answer - which is why this journey's third outcome is to hand over rather than to guess.

title: RSK-192 Risk signal → correlate evidence → clear, monitor, restrict or review
summary: Turn a measurement into a state change no larger than the evidence behind it supports, and no longer-lived than the question stays open.

distinctFrom.because: IDN-90 handles a specific suspicion - that an account is in someone else's hands - and runs a containment and recovery path for it. This is the general evidence lifecycle: most of what it sees clears, and its main job is not over-reacting.

This weighs uncertainty: how reliable the evidence is and what it supports, with no rule needing to have been broken for the question to be worth asking. RSK-194 starts only where an identifiable policy appears to have been breached, and tests that rule against the evidence and the version that governed it. A signal does not become a violation candidate by looking risky - without a governing rule to test, there is nothing for RSK-194 to decide.

title: RSK-193 Risk threshold crossed → apply scoped restriction → review or release
summary: Stop the smallest thing that manages the risk, and keep a stated route back.

distinctFrom.because: This determines what restriction the risk justifies and holds the release condition. ACC-78 applies and restores the access state. One is the reason, the other is the door.

title: RSK-194 Policy violation detected → validate → correct, restrict or escalate
summary: Establish that a rule was actually broken, against the version that governed it, before anything follows from that.

distinctFrom.because: DEC-186 handles what follows an authorized rejection. This determines whether a violation occurred at all and which consequence the policy defines - it may never reach a decision case, and most of its outcomes are corrections rather than refusals.

RSK-192 evaluates risk evidence without requiring any rule to have been broken, and most of what it sees clears. This starts from an identifiable governing rule and asks whether it was actually breached, judged against the version in force at the time. Risk evidence alone never opens a case here; it opens one there.

title: RSK-195 Compliance requirement → collect and verify → satisfied or blocked
summary: Hold one mandatory requirement as its own state, blocking only what genuinely depends on it.

distinctFrom.because: IDN-82 orchestrates collecting a verification and resuming what it blocked. This owns the compliance requirement as a business state - which requirement applies, whether existing evidence already satisfies it, and what happens when it cannot be met. It uses that collection mechanism rather than reimplementing one.

title: RSK-196 Compliance or policy hold → preserve state → resolve → resume or terminate
summary: Pause what a policy question makes unsafe, and leave everything else running.

distinctFrom.because: RSK-193 restricts because evidence of risk warrants it, and releases on evidence. A hold pauses because a policy or compliance question is open, and releases when that question is answered - the trigger, the authority and the release condition are all different.

title: RSK-197 Exception request → validate authority → approve, reject or review
summary: Ask for a controlled deviation from a named rule, over a stated scope, from someone entitled to ask.

distinctFrom.because: This defines what a policy exception is and whether one may even be sought - which rule, what scope, whose authority. Where the answer needs judgment it uses the decision engine rather than being one.

title: RSK-198 Exception granted → apply scoped override → expire or revoke
summary: Let an authorized deviation apply exactly where it was authorized, and stop applying the moment it should.

distinctFrom.because: RSK-197 establishes that a deviation is authorized. This is the runtime question - is it valid for this action, this entity, right now, and has it already been used up. An exception granted correctly and applied wrongly is still an unauthorized deviation.

title: RSK-199 Limit or quota reached → block, wait, increase or reset
summary: Treat a limit being reached as the limit working, and give the constrained action a real path forward.

distinctFrom.because: A limit is a constraint the entity was told about and is entitled to consume. Routing it into risk assessment puts ordinary heavy users in front of a fraud analyst, and produces a risk history for behaviour that was permitted.

title: RSK-200 Policy or risk state changed → re-evaluate affected work → resume, restrict or preserve
summary: Apply a change where the new authority actually reaches, and leave the past alone.

distinctFrom.because: RSK-191 evaluates one action at its decision point. This propagates a change across work already in flight, where the hard question is not what the rule says but which states the new rule is entitled to reach.

title: SCH-171 Availability query → evaluate capacity → offer valid options
summary: Produce the options that are genuinely bookable right now, and say plainly that nothing is being held.

distinctFrom.because: FUL-142 asks whether an accepted obligation can be resourced at all. This asks which specific times a resource can be committed to, for a requester who has not committed to anything yet.

title: SCH-172 Slot hold → reserve temporarily → confirm, expire or release
summary: Protect specific capacity for a bounded moment while a booking is being completed, without pretending it is a booking.

distinctFrom.because: FUL-143 allocates a resource to an obligation that already exists. This protects capacity for a commitment that does not exist yet and may never - most holds end in expiry rather than in a booking.

title: SCH-173 Reservation request → validate → confirm, reject or pending
summary: Turn a request for a specific time into a commitment both sides can rely on, or say clearly that it did not.

distinctFrom.because: FUL-141 creates a generic fulfillment obligation. This creates a commitment to a specific time on both sides - which is why it revalidates capacity at the moment of confirming and why its failure mode is contention rather than eligibility.

title: SCH-174 Reservation confirmed → prepare → upcoming or ready
summary: Get the conditions for a successful service in place, without letting them move the time that was promised.

title: SCH-175 Reschedule request → recheck availability → move, reject or preserve original
summary: Move a commitment to a new time without ever leaving the customer holding neither.

distinctFrom.because: SUB-166 changes the terms of a continuing relationship. This moves one specific occurrence to a different time or resource, and its whole difficulty is contention for the replacement - which terms changes never have.

title: SCH-176 Reservation cancellation → stop commitment → release capacity → reconcile
summary: End a future time commitment cleanly, returning the capacity and leaving the money to be decided elsewhere.

distinctFrom.because: FUL-150 cancels what remains of a generic fulfillment obligation. This ends a specific future time commitment, which releases capacity someone else can use and turns on timing relative to the appointment rather than on remaining scope.

title: SCH-177 Scheduled time approaches → revalidate → check in, start or exception
summary: Start a service from what the booking is now, not from a confirmation issued weeks ago.

title: SCH-178 Attendance or service start → complete, partial or interrupted
summary: Separate the fact that someone turned up from the question of whether they got what they came for.

title: SCH-179 No-show or missed appointment → validate → rebook, close or consequence
summary: Establish that one confirmed booking did not happen because the customer did not attend, having ruled out every other explanation.
